slides.title: Chapter 13: Web Scraping
slides.say: Welcome. This chapter follows a program from an address to a page it can read: the URL, the reply, the API, the HTML, and the browser it may have to drive. Every code slide shows the code, a plain explanation, and the result as a table, chart or diagram.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts: addresses and manners, opening and downloading, a weather API, reading HTML, and driving a browser. Each code slide has its place in the chapter-code tab of the page, in this same order.

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions to carry through the chapter. Which tool reaches which kind of page, and what decides the choice? And which printed outputs and programs of the book differ in current Python and on today's web?

slides.title: Part 1: Addresses and manners
slides.say: Part one. Before any download: an address has parts, a reply has a status code, a program has a name, and a site can say which paths it would rather not be crawled. Predict each answer before you read the result.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: addresses and manners
slides.say: A postal address is a good picture for a URL. HTTP is a postcard, HTTPS a sealed envelope. Ask students to add one more picture of their own.

slides.title: A URL is a scheme, a host, a path, a query and a fragment
slides.say: A URL is not one string but five parts. Urlsplit names them. Predict which part the server never receives, then check the fragment row.

slides.title: Percent codes and the query string
slides.say: A space and a comma may not stand in an address. Quote writes them as percent codes, parse_qs reads them back. Predict the encoded text before you run.

slides.title: HTTP status codes: the first digit is the class
slides.say: The first digit of a status code is its class: two for success, three for redirection, four for the client's fault, five for the server's. Which class is a 429?

slides.title: The user agent tells a server who is asking
slides.say: Python's downloader announces itself as Python-urllib, and a site may refuse it. A polite program sets its own name and a contact address.

slides.title: robots.txt: the paths a crawler is asked to avoid
slides.say: A robots.txt file lists paths a crawler is asked to avoid. The parser answers true or false. It is a request and not a lock, so honour it.

slides.title: Story: a courtesy file for robots, 30 June 1994
slides.say: Martijn Koster wrote down the consensus of 30 June 1994. The file is a courtesy, not a lock: the text itself says nobody enforces it. Ask students: what would you do if a site asked you not to crawl a path?

slides.title: A polite crawler waits between pages
slides.say: Some sites state a pause in their robots file. The fake clock shows the schedule without waiting. Predict the time of the third fetch.

slides.title: Story: the first spider counted 130 sites, 1993
slides.say: Matthew Gray built the first spider in 1993 to count the Web. 130 sites in June 1993, 100,000 by January 1996. Our link loop is the same idea at toy scale: fetch, find links, follow, repeat.

slides.title: Part 2: Opening and downloading
slides.say: Part two. Three ways to get at a page: ask the browser to show it, download it, or download it in chunks. The standard library stands in for requests so that every example runs on this page.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: opening a page with webbrowser
slides.say: The webbrowser module is the simplest tool of the chapter. It only opens a page in your own browser and cannot read it.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: downloading with requests
slides.say: Requests is the courier of the chapter. It brings the parcel, and raise_for_status reads the slip. Chunks let a huge parcel arrive box by box.

slides.title: webbrowser.open asks your own browser to show a page
slides.say: On this page the open call is replaced by a recorder so that no window opens. The real call returns true when a browser started and cannot read the page.

slides.title: Project 6: a map address from the command line
slides.say: Project six. The words typed after the script name become an address, which is percent-encoded and added to a search address. Predict the encoded text.

slides.title: Fetching a page: the reply has a type and a body
slides.say: A data address holds its text inside the address, so urlopen needs no network. The reply has a content type and a body of bytes.

slides.title: Story: Requests, conceived in frustration, 13 February 2011
slides.say: Requests was conceived on 13 February 2011 and born the next day. The version history still says Frustration, Conception, Birth. Ask students what frustrated him: network errors, routing and compression.

slides.title: raise_for_status stops the program on a bad reply
slides.say: Call raise_for_status after every download. A good reply passes quietly, a bad reply stops the program before it saves an error page as a file.

slides.title: iter_content: save a download in chunks
slides.say: Iter_content hands out a body in pieces. The write calls return the byte counts. Predict the last chunk, which is shorter.

slides.title: Part 3: A weather API
slides.say: Part three. A weather service answers in JSON. We read the reply, convert Kelvin, and build the address with a hidden key. A key is a password.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: a weather API
slides.say: An API is a menu. The key is a membership card: never print it in a log and never commit it to a repository.

slides.title: An API answers in JSON; json.loads turns it into data
slides.say: A web API answers in JSON text. Json.loads turns it into dictionaries and lists. Read the data one key or position at a time.

slides.title: The API gives Kelvin; the program converts
slides.say: The weather API reports Kelvin. Subtract 273.15 for Celsius, then convert to Fahrenheit. The chapter prints 12.3 and 54.1 for 285.44 Kelvin.

slides.title: An endpoint, its parameters and a secret key
slides.say: An endpoint is one address of a service. The key is a parameter, so it travels inside the address. Log the address only with the key hidden.

slides.title: Part 4: Reading HTML
slides.say: Part four. HTML is a tree of elements. We list its tags, pick elements by a path, avoid regular expressions, and resolve the links that a page holds. Two of the book's projects use these steps.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: reading HTML
slides.say: Seven pictures for reading HTML. The selector is an address for an element, and the developer tools show the boxes inside a page.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: picking things out of a page
slides.say: Select, get_text and get are the three moves of Beautiful Soup. The two projects use them to open results and to walk back through a comic series.

slides.title: HTML is nested tags with attributes
slides.say: HTML is nested tags with attributes. The parser calls a method for each opening tag. Predict which tag has no attributes.

slides.title: Pick elements by a path, read their text and attributes
slides.say: Beautiful Soup is not in the standard library, so ElementTree plays its part. The same three moves: select, get text, get an attribute.

slides.title: Story: Beautiful Soup, for pages somebody else wrote, 2004
slides.say: Leonard Richardson has kept Beautiful Soup since 2004. His promise: you did not write that awful page, you only want data from it. That is why we use a parser and not a regular expression.

slides.title: Do not read HTML with a regular expression
slides.say: The pattern needs href right after the tag name. The second link has a class first. A parser reads attributes by name and finds both.

slides.title: Practice program: link verification
slides.say: Practice program. Make links absolute, drop the fragment, skip other sites and count each page once. Predict how many pages remain.

slides.title: Project 8: the image and the Prev link of a comic page
slides.say: Project eight relies on the page structure of the comic site. The image address begins with two slashes, so urljoin borrows the scheme. Prev leads to the previous comic.

slides.title: Project 7: open the first results in browser tabs
slides.say: Project seven. Select all result links, keep the first few and open each one. A recording stand-in replaces the real open call.

slides.title: Part 5: Driving a browser
slides.say: Part five. Some pages are written by a script after the download. Then only a real browser helps: Selenium or Playwright. We build small stand-ins to see how they behave.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: driving a browser with Selenium
slides.say: Selenium drives a real browser from outside. Find_element and find_elements differ in what they do when nothing matches.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: driving a browser with Playwright
slides.say: Playwright starts with a context manager, opens a page, goes to an address and uses locators that wait. Browsers are installed by a second step.

slides.title: Why a download is not enough: pages built by a script
slides.say: The downloaded source holds an empty element and a script. A parser cannot read what the script writes. A real browser can, even headless.

slides.title: Story: Selenium began as a test runner for a timesheet, 2004
slides.say: Selenium began in 2004 at ThoughtWorks as a test tool for a timesheet application. Later it merged with WebDriver. The browser is driven from outside, which is why a driver is needed.

slides.title: Selenium: find_element fails, find_elements does not
slides.say: A stand-in for the Selenium driver. Find_elements returns a list that may be empty, find_element returns the first match and fails when there is none.

slides.title: Playwright: start, new page, goto, locator
slides.say: The same four steps as the chapter's program: start, new page, goto, locator. The real program also launches a browser first.

slides.title: Story: Playwright reached Python on 30 September 2020
slides.say: Arjun Attam announced Playwright for Python in preview on 30 September 2020. Its first promise is automatic waiting, which our last example imitates. Ask students why waiting matters on a slow page.

slides.title: Interacting with a page: wait until the element is there
slides.say: Playwright looks again until the element is ready. Selenium's find_element looks once. Predict the result with five looks and with two.

slides.title: Which tool for which page?
slides.say: Choose the tool by the page in front of the program. Webbrowser to show it, requests to fetch it, an API when there is one, a parser for static HTML, a browser driver only when a script builds the page.

slides.title: Current Python and today's web change more
slides.say: Python and the tools move on. The robots parser reads wildcard rules since Python 3.14.5. Selenium finds its driver by itself. Playwright needs a second install step. Run what the book printed, then check what changed.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep. The chart counts the code examples in each part of this deck.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills and a project. Predict first, then run what you can on the page. Ask students to explain each answer in one sentence.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Start with the book chapter, then the Python documentation, the documents of the four tools and the two protocol texts. The stories link to first-hand sources. Choose one link and read it before the next class.
